payload.name: resonant-peak
payload.scope: To quantify the maximum amplification in a closed-loop system's frequency response, so designers can assess relative stability and predict time-domain ringing.

definition.body: Resonant-peak is a human-made stability measure that quantifies the maximum magnitude of a closed-loop system's frequency response, occurring at the resonant frequency where the amplification is greatest. Parameters: (1) the closed-loop transfer function T(jw) = G(jw)/(1 + G(jw)H(jw)); (2) the resonant frequency wr where the magnitude of T(jw) achieves its maximum; (3) the peak magnitude Mr = max of the magnitude of T(jw) over all frequencies. For a standard second-order underdamped system, Mr = 1/(2*zeta*sqrt(1-zeta^2)) and wr = wn*sqrt(1-2*zeta^2), where zeta is the damping ratio, providing a direct quantitative link between frequency-domain amplification and time-domain transient quality. It is distinct from bandwidth (the frequency span where the gain exceeds -3 dB, not the maximum gain), gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, a different stability measure), and peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance of the steady-state value, not the frequency-domain amplification). Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard relative-stability specification in classical control engineering - measured from the Bode magnitude curve of closed-loop frequency responses, computed from analytical transfer functions, and specified in design requirements for servo systems, filter design, and vibration control - encoded in control textbooks (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Franklin, Powell, and Workman's Digital Control of Dynamic Systems), simulation tools, and aerospace control design practice. e.g.: the resonant peak Mr = 1.15 of a second-order system with zeta=0.5, attained at wr = 0.71wn; the closed-loop peak of a second-order low-pass filter with zeta=0.4 read from the Bode magnitude curve as Mr = 1.36; the design guideline bounding Mr below 1.5 to limit step overshoot, per Ogata's Modern Control Engineering | not: bandwidth (the passband width, not the peak gain); gain-margin (the gain headroom at the -180 degree phase crossing, not the peak magnitude); peak-overshoot (the time-domain exceedance, not the frequency-domain amplification) [formal: culminans amplificatio | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: controllability
payload.scope: To provide a formal criterion for whether a system's inputs can steer its internal state to any desired value, so engineers can verify that control design is structurally feasible before investing in gain tuning.

definition.body: Controllability is a human-made mathematical concept that maps the reachability property of a dynamical system's state space through its input channels. The construct determines whether, for a linear time-invariant system described by ẋ = Ax + Bu, there exists an input function u(t) over a finite time interval that can drive the state from any initial condition to any final state. The standard test constructs the controllability matrix with columns B, AB, A²B through Aⁿ⁻¹B and checks whether its rank equals n, the state dimension. If rank is less than n, the system has uncontrollable modes — state directions that no input can affect. The concept persists through control theory pedagogy (taught in every linear systems course), engineering design checklists (verifying controllability before designing state-feedback controllers), and software tools (MATLAB's ctrb and iscontrollable functions). It is distinct from observability (state reconstruction from outputs), stabilizability (uncontrollable modes are stable), and detectability (observability analogue for stabilization). e.g.: controllability check for a mass-spring system with single force input; full-rank controllability matrix of a 3-state aircraft longitudinal model; uncontrollable mode in parallel RLC circuit with voltage source across capacitor | not: observability (reconstructing state from outputs, not driving via inputs); stabilizability (allowing uncontrollable modes only if stable); reachability (stronger: attainable in exactly the specified time) [formal: controllabilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: stabilizability
payload.scope: To provide a relaxed controllability criterion that allows uncontrollable modes when they are naturally stable, enabling practical controller design for systems that are not fully controllable.

definition.body: Stabilizability is a human-made mathematical concept that relaxes the full controllability requirement by permitting uncontrollable modes so long as they are inherently stable. For a linear time-invariant system ẋ = Ax + Bu, the system is stabilizable if all uncontrollable modes have negative real parts — meaning the states that no input can affect decay naturally to zero. Equivalently, there exists a state-feedback matrix K such that A − BK has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane. The construct is distinguished from full controllability (which requires all modes to be input-affectable), observability (reconstruction from outputs), and detectability (the dual property for output injection). Stabilizability is the standard assumption under which pole-placement and LQR controller design proceed in practice, since real-world systems often have uncontrollable but stable modes. The concept persists through control theory textbooks, controller synthesis procedures, and aerospace/robotics design standards where full controllability is rarely achievable but stabilizability is verified. e.g.: verifying that an under-actuated quadcopter with only 4 actuators for 6 DOF has stabilizable lateral dynamics; checking eigenvalues of uncontrollable modes in a power grid small-signal model before designing a PSS; designing LQR gains for a robot arm model where gravity-induced coupling creates one stable uncontrollable mode | not: controllability (requires all modes input-affectable, not just stable ones); observability (reconstructing state from outputs); detectability (dual: all unobservable modes are stable) [formal: stabilibilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pole-placement
payload.scope: To provide a systematic procedure for designing state-feedback controllers by selecting gain matrices that place closed-loop poles at desired locations, ensuring stability and performance specifications are met.

definition.body: Pole-placement is a human-made control synthesis procedure that selects a state-feedback gain matrix K such that the closed-loop system matrix A − BK has eigenvalues at designer-specified locations in the complex plane. The construct maps the controllability of a state-space model to achievable pole positions: if the system is controllable, all pole locations are assignable; if only stabilizable, only unstable poles can be moved to stable locations. The standard algorithm (Ackermann's formula for SISO systems, or numerical methods like Bass-Gura and Kautsky-Nichols-Van Dooren for MIMO) computes K given the desired characteristic polynomial. The concept persists through control engineering practice (standard design procedure for single-loop state-feedback), aerospace flight control design (autopilot pole assignment), robotics trajectory control, and software implementations (MATLAB's place and acker functions). It is distinct from LQR (which optimizes a quadratic cost rather than specifying pole locations directly), from pole-zero cancellation (which uses plant zeros rather than feedback to shape response), and from root-locus (which traces pole migration as gain varies rather than prescribing exact locations). e.g.: placing closed-loop poles at s=-2 and s=-3 for a second-order mass-spring system to achieve zeta=0.707; using MATLAB's place function to assign 6 poles for an aircraft pitch controller; Ackermann's formula for a 3-state DC motor speed control system | not: LQR (optimizes quadratic cost, does not prescribe exact pole locations); root-locus (visualizes pole migration with gain variation, not exact placement); pole-zero cancellation (uses plant dynamics, not feedback gain selection) [formal: dispositio polaris | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lqr
payload.scope: To compute optimal state-feedback control by minimizing a weighted quadratic cost, balancing state regulation against control effort, producing gains that guarantee stability margins and robustness.

definition.body: LQR (Linear Quadratic Regulator) is a human-made optimal control synthesis procedure that computes a state-feedback gain matrix by minimizing a quadratic performance index. The construct selects K to minimize J = integral of (x^T Q x + u^T R u) dt, where x is the state, u = -Kx is the control, Q is a positive semi-definite state weighting, and R is a positive definite input weighting. The solution solves the algebraic Riccati equation A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0, yielding K = R^{-1} B^T P. The persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard optimal control design in aerospace, robotics, and industrial process control — encoded in control theory textbooks (Franklin, Powell, and Workman; Anderson and Moore), optimization software, and real-time controller implementations in flight control systems, autonomous vehicles, and process plants. It is distinct from pole-placement (which specifies exact pole locations without optimizing a cost), from LQG (LQR combined with a Kalman filter for noisy measurements), and from MPC (model predictive control, which optimizes over a finite horizon with constraints). e.g.: LQR gains for a satellite attitude control system with Q = diag(1,1,0.1,0.1) and R = 0.01; a quadcopter altitude controller with weight trade-offs between position error and motor effort; the LQR-optimal damping of a turbine generator swing equation to minimize oscillation energy | not: pole-placement (specifies exact pole locations, does not optimize a quadratic cost); LQG (LQR with Kalman filter for output feedback under noise); MPC (optimizes over finite horizon with constraints, not infinite-horizon quadratic) [formal: regulatio quadratica linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: state-observer
payload.scope: To estimate the internal state of a system from its outputs, enabling state-feedback control when full state measurement is unavailable.

definition.body: A state-observer is a human-made dynamical system that estimates the internal state variables of a plant from measurable inputs and outputs. The construct replicates the plant dynamics and adds an injection term proportional to the output error: the observer equation is x̂̇ = A x̂ + Bu + L(y - ŷ), where x̂ is the estimated state, L is the observer gain, y is the measured output, and ŷ = C x̂ is the estimated output. The estimation error e = x - x̂ evolves as ė = (A - LC)e, so the observer gain L is chosen to place the eigenvalues of A-LC in the left half-plane for convergence. The persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard state-estimation technique in control engineering — encoded in control theory textbooks (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, and Workman), observer synthesis tools, and real-time implementations in motor control, aerospace, and robotics where full state sensors are impractical or too costly. The construct is distinguished from the Kalman filter (stochastic estimation minimizing error variance under noise), the Luenberger observer (deterministic full-order special case), and the sliding-mode observer (discontinuous injection for robustness against matched uncertainties). e.g.: full-order observer for a DC motor estimating angular velocity from encoder position only; aircraft attitude observer fusing GPS and IMU data to reconstruct all six state variables; observer-based state-feedback control of a robotic manipulator measuring only joint positions | not: Kalman filter (stochastic optimal estimation minimizing error variance under noise models); Luenberger observer (deterministic full-order special case, not a separate construct); sliding-mode observer (uses discontinuous injection for robustness against matched uncertainties) [formal: observator statuum | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: riccati-equation
payload.scope: To provide a nonlinear matrix equation whose solution yields optimal feedback gains for linear systems with quadratic cost, and whose stability characterizations underpin Lyapunov theory in control and estimation.

definition.body: The Riccati equation is a human-made nonlinear matrix equation of the form A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0 (continuous-time algebraic Riccati equation, or CARE), where A is the state matrix, B is the input matrix, Q is a symmetric positive semi-definite state-weighting matrix, and R is a symmetric positive definite input-weighting matrix, and P is the unknown symmetric matrix to be solved for. A discrete-time variant exists: A^T P A - P - (A^T P B)(R + B^T P B)^{-1}(B^T P A) + Q = 0. Parameters: matrices A, B, Q, R defining the system and cost; the solution matrix P. The equation persists as a computational object in optimal control synthesis, filter design (Kalman filter gain computation), differential game theory, and robust control — encoded in numerical software (MATLAB's care/dare, SciPy's solve_continuous_are), control theory textbooks (Anderson & Moore, Lancaster & Rodman), and aerospace/robotics design tools. e.g.: MATLAB's care function computing P for a quadcopter LQR design with Q=diag(1,1,0.1,0.1) and R=0.01*I; the CARE solution for a satellite attitude control problem yielding optimal gains for reaction wheel actuation; SciPy's solve_continuous_are applied to a DC motor velocity regulator with state weights for position and speed | not: linear matrix equation (linear in the unknown, not nonlinear quadratic); Lyapunov equation (A^T P + P A = -Q is the special case with no B R^{-1} B^T P term, i.e. R^{-1}=0) [formal: aequatio Riccati | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lyapunov-equation
payload.scope: To provide a linear matrix equation whose solvability characterizes asymptotic stability of linear dynamical systems, forming the algebraic backbone of Lyapunov stability theory.

definition.body: The Lyapunov equation is a human-made linear matrix equation of the form A^T P + P A = -Q (continuous-time), where A is the state matrix, Q is a given symmetric positive-definite matrix, and P is the unknown symmetric matrix to be solved for. A discrete-time variant exists: A^T P A - P = -Q. Parameters: matrices A and Q. The Lyapunov equation persists as a computational tool in stability analysis — the Lyapunov theorem states that a linear system is asymptotically stable iff for every positive-definite Q, the equation has a unique positive-definite solution P. Encoded in MATLAB lyap, SciPy solve_lyapunov, control theory textbooks (Khalil; Lancaster & Rodman). e.g.: MATLAB lyap verifying stability of A=[0 1; -5 -2]; SciPy solve_lyapunov for aircraft longitudinal dynamics; Lyapunov equation for power grid small-signal model | not: algebraic Riccati equation (nonlinear quadratic variant with feedback term); Sylvester equation (A X + X B = C is more general, Lyapunov is B=A^T, C=-Q) [formal: aequatio Lyapunov | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lqg
payload.scope: To provide optimal state-feedback combined with optimal state estimation when only noisy outputs are available, separating the design into independent LQR and Kalman-filter components.

definition.body: LQG (Linear Quadratic Gaussian) is a human-made optimal control synthesis procedure that combines an LQR state-feedback controller with a Kalman filter state estimator, using the separation principle: the control gain and estimator gain are designed independently and then combined into an output-feedback controller. Parameters: the LQR cost matrices (Q, R), the Kalman noise covariances (process noise W, measurement noise V), system matrices (A, B, C), and the resulting gain matrices (K for feedback, L for estimation). The closed-loop output is u = -K x_hat where x_hat is the Kalman-filter estimate. LQG persists as the standard linear stochastic control design method -- encoded in control textbooks (Kailath; Anderson & Moore), MATLAB lqg function, and industrial applications in aerospace guidance, robotics, and process control where states are unmeasurable. e.g.: MATLAB lqg design for a satellite attitude controller with LQR gains and Kalman filter for star-tracker outputs; LQG control of a quadcopter with IMU measurements feeding a Kalman observer; LQG-based autopilot for a fixed-wing aircraft using GPS position and barometer altitude as noisy measurements | not: LQR (no noise estimation, uses full state feedback only); Kalman filter alone (estimation only, not combined with optimal control); MPC (finite-horizon constrained optimization, not infinite-horizon stochastic) [formal: regulatio quadratica linearis gaussiana | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.note: A lag-compensator is a controller transfer function that modifies the loop gain of a feedback loop. It only operates within the context of a feedback loop structure — its purpose is to shape the loop gain L(s)=G(s)H(s) by boosting low-frequency gain while adding minimal phase lag near crossover. Remove the feedback-loop construct and a lag-compensator has no loop in which to operate: its transfer-function modification has no target. A state-observer reconstructs internal states from measured outputs. The entire concept of state reconstruction is grounded in the observability property: an observer can only reconstruct states that are observable from the outputs. The observability matrix [C; CA; CA^2; ...] determines which state directions are reconstructable. Remove the concept of observability and a state-observer has no criterion for whether its estimation is possible — there is no way to know if the observer error dynamics converge for the full state or only for observable modes. Direction: state-observer (the estimation procedure) depends on observability (the property that determines what can be estimated).

State-observers are designed under the detectability assumption: unobservable modes must be naturally stable for the observer to be useful. The observer gain L is chosen to place eigenvalues of A-LC in the left half-plane, but this can only be done for the observable modes — detectability guarantees that the remaining unobservable modes are already stable. Remove the concept of detectability and there is no criterion for whether a given system admits a stable observer design. The removal test passes: without detectability, an observer designer has no basis for deciding whether the system is suitable for observation. Direction: state-observer (the design) depends on detectability (the property ensuring observer stability).

A state-observer estimates internal states from outputs. While observability determines whether estimation is possible in principle, controllability determines whether the plant itself has input channels that affect all state directions. A state-observer design must account for controllability because the observer and controller are often co-designed (separation principle): the combined observer-controller requires both controllability and observability for full closed-loop stability. Remove controllability from the map and the state-observer loses its context for how the estimated states will be used — the observer estimates states that a controller will manipulate via input channels, and controllability defines which state directions those input channels can reach. Direction: state-observer depends on controllability for its full design context.

A lag-compensator modifies the loop gain L(s) of a feedback system. Its entire purpose is to shape the loop gain: increasing low-frequency gain to reduce steady-state error while adding minimal phase lag near crossover to preserve stability margins. The compensator transfer function is designed as a modification to L(s). Remove the concept of loop-gain and a lag-compensator has no target quantity to modify — its design specifications (gain boost ratio α, lag center frequency, phase lag at crossover) are all defined relative to the loop gain. The removal test passes: without loop-gain, the compensator is just an isolated transfer function with no design target. Direction: lag-compensator depends on loop-gain.

LQR computes optimal state-feedback gains by minimizing a quadratic cost. The existence theorem states that LQR produces a stabilizing controller if and only if the system is stabilizable. Remove the concept of stabilizability and LQR loses its existence guarantee: there is no criterion telling the designer whether the resulting closed-loop system will be stable. The Riccati equation solution may still exist mathematically, but without stabilizability there is no guarantee it yields stabilizing gains. The removal test passes: stabilizability is the structural condition under which LQR works. Direction: lqr depends on stabilizability.

Gain-crossover-frequency is defined as the frequency where |L(jω)| = 1 (0 dB). This magnitude is a value on the frequency response curve of the loop gain L(s). Remove the concept of frequency-response and the gain-crossover frequency has no curve on which to be defined — it is a specific point (unity-magnitude crossing) on a broader function (the frequency response). The removal test passes: without frequency-response, there is no magnitude-vs-frequency function to find the unity crossing on. Direction: gain-crossover-frequency depends on frequency-response.

payload.name: state-feedback
payload.scope: To shape a system's internal dynamics directly, by computing the control input as a function of the state vector, so that one gain matrix can place the closed-loop poles.

definition.body: State-feedback is a human-made control architecture in which the control input is computed directly from the system's state vector: u(t) = -K x(t), where x is the complete description of the internal state and K is the feedback gain matrix. Where the state is not fully measured, the command uses an observer's estimate: u = -K x_hat. Parameters: (1) the state vector x, or its estimate x_hat; (2) the gain matrix K (n by m), designed to place the eigenvalues of A-BK; (3) the state source, full measurement or a state-observer estimate (observer-based state-feedback). It is distinct from output-feedback (the command is computed from the measured output y, as in a PID or a lead-lag compensator), from feedforward (the command is shaped from the reference with no state), and from the state-observer (estimation only, no control law). Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard design form of modern control, pole-placement and LQR both producing exactly this K, implemented in flight control, robotics, and process control, and encoded in control textbooks (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, and Workman) and MATLAB's place and lqr. e.g.: pole-placement speed controller for a DC motor with K from Ackermann's formula; satellite attitude controller with LQR gain K from the estimated state; robot-manipulator torque command u = -K x_hat with x_hat from a Luenberger observer | not: output-feedback PID on the measured error (the controller reads y, not x_hat); feedforward control shaped from the reference with no state; the state-observer (the estimator alone, no control law) [formal: retroactio statuum | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: separation-principle
payload.scope: To permit independent design of a state observer and a state-feedback controller, then combine them while preserving the eigenvalue structure of both.

definition.body: The separation principle states that the design of a state-observer and a state-feedback controller for a linear system can be performed independently, and the combined observer-controller yields a closed-loop system whose eigenvalues are the union of the observer and controller eigenvalues. Parameters: (1) a linear time-invariant plant with state-space matrices A, B, C; (2) observer gain L chosen to place eigenvalues of A-LC; (3) feedback gain K chosen to place eigenvalues of A-BK. Theorem: the eigenvalues of the combined (A-BK) and (A-LC) dynamics are exactly the union of the two sets, so the observer and controller may be tuned separately. Persistence mechanism: encoded as a fundamental theorem of modern control theory, taught in all standard texts (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, Workman) and used as the design methodology in every observer-based control implementation. e.g.: design of aircraft attitude controller with Luenberger observer gain and LQR gain tuned independently; robot manipulator with independently tuned observer and controller bandwidths | not: Kalman-Bucy filter (stochastic estimation with noise models, not deterministic separation); adaptive control (parameter estimation updates online, not deterministic separation) [formal: separatio principium | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: observer-controller
payload.scope: To combine state estimation and state-feedback into a single implementable control law, using estimated states for real-time control.

definition.body: An observer-controller is the combined construct of a state-observer and a state-feedback controller, designed via the separation principle. Parameters: (1) estimated state x_hat from an observer (e.g., Luenberger or Kalman); (2) control law u = -K x_hat applied to the estimated state; (3) combined dynamics with eigenvalues partitionable into observer eigenvalues (A-LC) and controller eigenvalues (A-BK). Persistence mechanism: encoded as the standard design methodology in control engineering, implemented in flight control systems, robotics, and aerospace applications, taught in control textbooks (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, Workman) and implemented in synthesis tools. e.g.: F-16 flight controller using Luenberger observer and LQR gain; satellite attitude control with Kalman filter and pole-placement gain; industrial robot manipulator with extended Kalman observer and state-feedback | not: output-feedback controller using measured output y directly (no observer); feedforward control from reference trajectory (no state estimation or feedback) [formal: observer-continens | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

definition.body: An observer-controller is the combined construct of a state-observer and a state-feedback controller, designed via the separation principle. Persistence mechanism: encoded as the standard design methodology in control engineering, implemented in flight control systems, robotics, and aerospace applications, taught in control textbooks (Ogata; Franklin, Powell, Workman) and implemented in synthesis tools. e.g.: F-16 flight controller using Luenberger observer and LQR gain; satellite attitude control with Kalman filter and pole-placement gain; industrial robot manipulator with extended Kalman observer and state-feedback | not: output-feedback controller using measured output y directly (no observer); feedforward control from reference trajectory (no state estimation or feedback) [formal: observer-continens | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

[3 test] The note's removal test shows a loss of criterion, not a stop of operation. The state-observer carve's own design step, in its own words: 'the observer gain L is chosen to place the eigenvalues of A-LC in the left half-plane for convergence.' That design step operates with or without the detectability concept on the map: for a system with unobservable unstable modes the eigenvalue placement simply cannot complete, and the designer sees that in the placement attempt itself. Detectability is the name of the existence condition - useful, and its own standing construct - but the note's stated consequence is 'there is no criterion for whether a given system admits a stable observer design': an epistemic loss, the same class as the loop-gain and step-response removals the board struck. Contrast the pole-placement edge, where the from-endpoint's OWN words name the condition ('if the system is controllable, all pole locations are assignable'); the state-observer carve names detectability nowhere. Item 3 fails: a loss of criterion is not a stop of operation.

[5 sense] Item 5 fails: the note uses the to-endpoint in a sense its accepted definition does not carve. The accepted observability entry carves 'a software engineering practice that defines how to determine the internal state of a running system from its external outputs - specifically logs (structured event records), metrics (quantified measurements over time), and traces (request journeys across services)', persisting through Prometheus, Grafana and Jaeger. That is the operational-engineering practice. The note instead argues from a control-theory property - 'the observability matrix [C; CA; CA^2; ...] determines which state directions are reconstructable' - a rank condition on state-space matrices that the accepted entry's carve contains nowhere. The note never pins a sense the accepted def supports; it simply reuses the word for a different construct. A control-theory observability property would need its own filing, and this edge cannot be judged against a definition that does not carve it. Item 3 fails as a consequence: the removal test is stated against a property the to-endpoint does not hold.

payload.name: control-theory-observability
payload.scope: To determine which internal states of a dynamical system can be reconstructed from its measured outputs over time.

definition.body: Observability in control theory is a property of a dynamical system that determines whether its internal states can be uniquely inferred from knowledge of its external outputs over a finite time interval. The construct distinguishes observable state directions (those reconstructable from output measurements) from unobservable ones. For a linear time-invariant system x_dot = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du, the system is observable if the observability matrix [C; CA; CA^2; ...; CA^{n-1}] has full rank n, where n is the state dimension. Parameters: (1) system matrices A and C that define the state evolution and output mapping, (2) the state dimension n, (3) the time horizon over which outputs are measured. It is distinct from controllability (whether states can be driven via inputs, not measured via outputs), from detectability (which relaxes observability by allowing stable unobservable modes), and from state estimation (the practical procedure that uses observability as its existence guarantee). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a fundamental analysis tool in control engineering — taught in every linear systems course, checked in aerospace and robotics design before state-feedback or observer synthesis, implemented in MATLAB (obsv, isrobust), and referenced in design standards for flight control and autonomous vehicle systems. e.g.: checking rank of observability matrix for a 4-state aircraft longitudinal model; determining that altitude and velocity are observable from GPS range measurements alone; verifying full-state observability of a DC motor from encoder position and current sensing | not: software observability (inferring internal state from logs, metrics, and traces in running software); detectability (allows unobservable modes if they are naturally stable); state estimation (the procedure that requires observability but is not the property itself) [formal: observabilitas (theoriae controli) | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.note: LQR design requires Lyapunov stability analysis: the closed-loop stability guarantee comes from Lyapunov's direct method. The Riccati equation solution P must be positive definite, and V(x) = x^T P x serves as a Lyapunov function proving asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system A-BK. Remove Lyapunov stability theory and LQR loses its stability guarantee — there is no mechanism to prove the closed-loop eigenvalues lie in the left half-plane. Direction: lqr depends on lyapunov-equation.
